title: Privity and third-party rights
subtitle: Who can sue on a contract they never signed
objectives: State the doctrine of privity and explain both of its limbs — who may sue, and who may be sued
Identify the common law devices developed to soften privity's effect before 1999, and their limits
Apply the conditions in the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 to determine whether a named third party can enforce a term

leadingAuthorities.citation: Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Co Ltd v Selfridge & Co Ltd [1915] AC 847
leadingAuthorities.role: Establishes the classic doctrine: a stranger to the contract can neither sue nor be sued on it
Shows privity's harshness in practice, and the narrow common law route around it — suing in a different capacity

leadingAuthorities.citation: Jackson v Horizon Holidays Ltd [1975] 1 WLR 1468
leadingAuthorities.role: A contracting party recovers damages measured by a third party's disappointment, an exceptional common law workaround

leadingAuthorities.citation: Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999, ss 1-2
leadingAuthorities.role: Statutory exception letting a named or identified third party enforce a term directly, subject to conditions

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Privity sounds abstract until you meet it in a problem question dressed as something else — a wedding gift, a building contract with subcontractors, a holiday booked for a family. Where the profile shows students can state the rule but stumble applying the 1999 Act's conditions, this note appears: 'You know privity exists — this lesson is about running the third-party enforcement test, condition by condition.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well here on the rule itself before. Most of the test pool below hands you a scenario and asks whether s 1 of the 1999 Act is satisfied — treat every fact as a condition to check off, not a story to react to.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and hold the two limbs of privity clearly in mind before moving on — everything from Part 2 onward assumes you can state the basic doctrine without hesitation.

overview.hook: Old Beswick promises his nephew the coal business, on condition the nephew pays a weekly annuity to his widow for the rest of her life. The nephew signs. The nephew stops paying. The widow — who signed nothing, agreed to nothing, gave no consideration for anything — goes to court to enforce a bargain she was never a party to. On the face of the law, she has no claim at all. This lesson is about why that's the starting position, and the increasingly elaborate ways the law found to escape it.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 22 September 2026. The common law doctrine and the 1999 Act are both settled; no reform is pending in this area.

parts.heading: A contract is a closed circle
parts.voice: expository — lays out the doctrine plainly before showing its bite, like a textbook chapter opening
body: Privity of contract is a deceptively simple idea: a contract creates rights and obligations only between the people who made it. A stranger to the agreement — however closely their life is touched by it — can neither sue to enforce it nor be sued for breaching it. Consideration and privity are historically tangled together in English law: the classic reasoning is that a third party has given nothing in exchange for the promise, so has no standing to enforce it.

The doctrine was settled definitively by the House of Lords in Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Co Ltd v Selfridge & Co Ltd. Dunlop sold tyres to a distributor, Dew & Co, on terms that Dew would extract a promise from any retailer it resold to not to sell below a fixed price. Selfridge bought from Dew, agreed to that price-maintenance term — and then broke it. Dunlop sued Selfridge directly.

The House of Lords held Dunlop's claim failed. Dunlop was not a party to the contract between Dew and Selfridge; it had given no consideration for Selfridge's promise. However closely Dunlop's commercial interest was bound up in that resale term, it stood outside the circle the contract drew, and the law gave it no claim.

Notice the doctrine has two edges, not one. It stops third parties enforcing benefits meant for them (Selfridge could not have been sued by Dunlop even if the boot were on the other foot in some hypothetical), and it stops third parties being burdened by obligations they never agreed to. Both limbs matter, but it is almost always the first — a third party locked out of a benefit — that drives the cases worth knowing.

components.definition: The common law rule that only the parties to a contract acquire rights or incur liabilities under it; a third party can neither sue on it nor be sued on it, whatever benefit or burden it was meant to carry for them.

components.caseName: Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Co Ltd v Selfridge & Co Ltd
components.factsShort: Dunlop tried to enforce a price-maintenance term against a retailer, Selfridge, with whom Dunlop had no direct contract — the term existed only in Selfridge's contract with an intermediate distributor.
components.ratioShort: A person who is not a party to a contract, and who has given no consideration for a promise in it, cannot sue to enforce that promise, however clearly it was meant to benefit them.

expanded.facts: Dunlop manufactured tyres and sold them to Dew & Co, a distributor, under a contract requiring Dew to obtain undertakings from any retailer buying from it that the retailer would not resell below Dunlop's list price and would pay Dunlop a penalty for breach. Selfridge bought tyres from Dew, gave that undertaking to Dew, and then sold below the fixed price. Dunlop sued Selfridge directly for breach of the price undertaking and for the contractual penalty.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Viscount Haldane LC stated the principle in terms that became the doctrine's classic formulation: only a person who is a party to a contract can sue on it, and 'a person who is not a party to a contract cannot take advantage of provisions in it, although the contract is made for his benefit'. He also tied the point to consideration — Dunlop had given no consideration for Selfridge's promise not to undercut the price.
expanded.significance: This is the foundational modern authority for privity in English law. Every workaround covered later in this lesson exists because Dunlop's result was widely seen as unjust in individual cases — the doctrine survived, but courts and eventually Parliament built routes around its edges rather than abandoning it.

interaction.prompt: In Dunlop v Selfridge, why did Dunlop's claim against Selfridge fail?
options: Dunlop was not a party to the contract containing the price term and had given no consideration for it
Selfridge had a valid defence of economic duress
The price-maintenance term was void for uncertainty
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Exactly right — privity and consideration work together here: no contract with Selfridge, no consideration from Dunlop, no standing to sue.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at who actually contracted with whom. Dunlop's contract was with Dew, not Selfridge — the price term touching Selfridge lived in a different contract entirely, one Dunlop was a stranger to.

parts.heading: Beswick's widow, and the narrowest of escape routes
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the human story in full before extracting the doctrine, letting the injustice land before the fix is explained
body: Peter Beswick ran a coal merchant's business. Old and wanting to retire, he transferred the business to his nephew John, on terms set out in a written agreement: John would employ Peter as a consultant for the rest of Peter's life, and after Peter's death would pay Peter's widow, Ruth, an annuity of £5 a week. Peter died. John paid Ruth once, then stopped.

Ruth sued — but she faced privity head-on. She was not a party to the agreement between Peter and John; the promise to pay her was made to Peter, for her benefit, but she herself had given no consideration and signed nothing. On Dunlop's logic, she had no claim in her own right at all.

Ruth's claim survived only because she happened to be the administratrix of Peter's estate — she could sue not as the intended beneficiary, but standing in Peter's shoes as his personal representative, enforcing the contract Peter himself had made. The House of Lords went further and held that damages alone would be inadequate (since the estate itself had suffered no real financial loss — it was Ruth personally who lost the annuity), and ordered specific performance instead, compelling John to make the payments Peter's contract required.

Look closely at what actually rescued Ruth: nothing about privity was relaxed. She won only because English procedure happened to let one person hold two legal identities — widow (no standing) and administratrix (full standing, as Peter's successor). Take away the administratrix appointment, and Beswick comes out exactly like Dunlop: the intended beneficiary loses.

components.factsShort: A nephew promised his uncle he would pay an annuity to the uncle's widow after the uncle's death, in exchange for the uncle's coal business. The nephew stopped paying; the widow, a stranger to the contract, sued.
components.ratioShort: The widow could not sue in her personal capacity as a third party, but could and did succeed by suing as administratrix of her late husband's estate, enforcing his own contractual rights — and was awarded specific performance because damages to the estate would have been nominal.

expanded.facts: Peter Beswick agreed to transfer his coal business to his nephew John in return for John's promise to employ Peter as a consultant during his lifetime and, after his death, to pay a weekly annuity to Peter's widow Ruth. John performed for a short time after Peter's death, then stopped paying. Ruth brought proceedings both in her personal capacity and as administratrix of Peter's estate.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The House of Lords confirmed that Ruth's personal claim failed on ordinary privity grounds — she was a third party who had given no consideration. But as administratrix, she stood in her late husband's position and could enforce the contract he had made. On remedy, the House held that damages recoverable by the estate would be merely nominal (the estate itself lost nothing measurable), so damages were an inadequate remedy — justifying the unusual step of ordering specific performance of a promise to pay money.
expanded.significance: Beswick is cited constantly precisely because it shows both the harshness of privity and the ingenuity required to avoid it. It is not authority for any general third-party right — it is authority that, where the beneficiary can also sue as the promisee's successor, specific performance may fill the gap damages cannot.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often summarise Beswick as 'the House of Lords let a third party enforce a contract made for her benefit'.
components.whyItsWrong: That overstates the case. Ruth did not succeed as a third party at all — her personal claim on that basis failed. She succeeded only because she also held the separate, unrelated status of administratrix, allowing her to enforce Peter's own contractual right rather than any right of her own.

interaction.prompt: Put the key events and legal steps in Beswick v Beswick in order.
items: Peter transfers the coal business to John in return for a promise to pay Ruth an annuity
John stops paying the annuity after Peter's death
Ruth's personal claim as the intended beneficiary fails for want of privity
Ruth succeeds instead as administratrix of Peter's estate, and is granted specific performance
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the shape of the case exactly — and notice the pivot at step 3 to step 4: the same person, suing in a different capacity, gets a completely different result.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again, particularly around Ruth's two attempts to sue — one fails, and it is only the second, different capacity that succeeds. That pivot is the whole point of the case.

parts.heading: Someone else's loss, on your own claim
parts.voice: wry and slightly skeptical — treats the doctrine as a legal fiction worth being honest about, inviting the reader to notice the sleight of hand
body: Here is a puzzle: if Beswick's route depends on holding a second legal identity, what happens when no such identity is available — when the contracting party is simply a contracting party, and the person who actually suffers is someone else entirely, with no estate to stand behind?

Jackson v Horizon Holidays gives one answer, and it is a slightly uncomfortable one. Mr Jackson booked a family holiday for himself, his wife, and their children. The holiday was a disaster — nothing like the brochure promised. Mr Jackson sued Horizon Holidays for breach of contract. The difficulty was that most of the misery had been suffered not by him personally but by his family, who were not parties to the booking contract at all.

The Court of Appeal allowed Mr Jackson to recover damages reflecting the disappointment and distress of the whole family, not just his own. Lord Denning's reasoning treated the contracting party as recovering, in substance, for the loss suffered by those he had contracted for — a legal fiction that lets the third parties' loss travel inside the contracting party's own claim, without ever giving the third parties a cause of action of their own.

Be precise about what Jackson does and doesn't do. It does not give the family a right to sue Horizon Holidays themselves — they still have none. It lets the one person who does have a claim recover a larger sum than his own personal disappointment alone would justify. It is a workaround aimed at the promisor's pocket, not a recognition of third-party rights, and later cases have treated its reasoning as exceptional rather than a general licence to sue for other people's losses.

components.factsShort: Mr Jackson booked a family holiday that fell far short of what was promised; he alone had contracted with the holiday company, but his family suffered most of the disappointment.
components.ratioShort: A contracting party can recover damages reflecting the loss and disappointment suffered by third parties for whom the contract was made, without those third parties acquiring any claim of their own.

expanded.facts: Mr Jackson booked a holiday in Ceylon for himself, his wife and their two young children, based on a glowing brochure description. The accommodation and facilities were substantially worse than described. Mr Jackson sued Horizon Holidays for breach of contract, claiming damages that reflected the distress suffered by the whole family, not just himself.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal upheld a damages award that went beyond Mr Jackson's own personal disappointment, treating him as entitled to recover for the loss of enjoyment suffered by the family as a whole, on the basis that the contract was plainly made for their collective benefit even though only he was a party to it.
expanded.significance: Jackson is the clearest common law example of damages, rather than any direct right of action, being used to route relief to third parties. It has been treated cautiously in later cases (including doubts about how far its reasoning survives independently of the 1999 Act) but remains a leading illustration of the pre-statutory workarounds.

components.term: Damages for a third party's loss
components.definition: An exceptional common law measure, illustrated by Jackson, under which a contracting party's own damages award can reflect loss actually suffered by third parties the contract was made to benefit — without those third parties gaining any right to sue.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that Jackson v Horizon Holidays gave Mr Jackson's family a direct right to sue Horizon Holidays?
sliderLabels: Confident it did give them a direct right
interaction.explanation: It did not. The family never acquired any cause of action — Jackson only enlarged the damages recoverable by Mr Jackson himself, the one person who had actually contracted with Horizon Holidays.

parts.heading: Parliament's fix: the 1999 Act
parts.voice: structural — a precise, checklist-driven walk through the statutory test, built for students to return to when applying it
body: By the late twentieth century, the Law Commission concluded that the common law's patchwork of workarounds — agency, trust of a promise, Jackson-style damages — was too unpredictable to be a satisfactory answer to privity's unfairness. Parliament responded with the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999, which creates a direct, if conditional, right for a third party to enforce a term.

Section 1(1) sets the gateway. A third party may enforce a term of a contract if either (a) the contract expressly provides that they may, or (b) the term purports to confer a benefit on them — subject to section 1(2), which blocks enforcement under limb (b) where, on a proper construction of the contract, the parties did not intend the term to be enforceable by the third party. Limb (a) is a deliberate opt-in; limb (b) is a rebuttable presumption in the third party's favour once a benefit is identified.

Section 1(3) then imposes an identification requirement: the third party must be expressly named in the contract, or identified as a member of a class, or answering a particular description — but need not be in existence when the contract is made, which is what lets a contract benefit an as-yet-unborn grandchild or a company not yet incorporated.

Section 2 protects the third party's right once it has arisen: broadly, once the third party has relied on the term, or the promisor knows of that reliance, or the promisor can reasonably be expected to have foreseen it, the original contracting parties cannot rescind or vary the contract to remove or diminish that right without the third party's consent — subject to any express term of the contract saying otherwise. The Act is also, importantly, a default regime: contracting parties remain free to exclude it entirely by clear words, and commercial contracts very often do exactly that.

components.citation: Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999, s 1(1)-(3)
components.text: (1) Subject to the provisions of this Act, a person who is not a party to a contract (a 'third party') may in his own right enforce a term of the contract if— (a) the contract expressly provides that he may, or (b) subject to subsection (2), the term purports to confer a benefit on him. (2) Subsection (1)(b) does not apply if on a proper construction of the contract it appears that the parties did not intend the term to be enforceable by the third party. (3) The third party must be expressly identified in the contract by name, as a member of a class or as answering a particular description but need not be in existence when the contract is entered into.
elements: Third party is not a party to the contract
Either express provision for enforcement, OR a term purporting to confer a benefit (unless the parties did not so intend)
Third party expressly identified by name, class, or description
Third party need not exist yet when the contract is made

components.label: Running the s 1 test
points: Step 1 — Is the claimant a third party to the contract at all? If they are already a party, s 1 is irrelevant.
Step 2 — Does the contract expressly say the third party may enforce the term? If yes, s 1(1)(a) is satisfied outright.
Step 3 — If not, does the term purport to confer a benefit on the third party? A term that merely happens to benefit them incidentally is not enough.
Step 4 — Even if a benefit is identified, check s 1(2): did the parties, on the contract's proper construction, actually intend the term to be enforceable by the third party?
Step 5 — Is the third party identified by name, class, or description under s 1(3)? They need not exist yet.
Step 6 — Check for an express exclusion clause: many commercial contracts contract out of the 1999 Act altogether.

interaction.prompt: Under s 1(3) of the 1999 Act, which of the following is required for a third party to be capable of enforcing a term?
options: The third party must already exist and be named individually — classes and unborn beneficiaries are excluded
The third party must be expressly identified by name, as a member of a class, or by description, but need not exist yet
The third party must have given some consideration for the term, even if less than the promisor received
interaction.feedback: Correct — s 1(3) deliberately allows identification by class or description, and expressly removes any need for the third party to be in existence at the time of contracting, which is what makes the Act useful for unborn beneficiaries or future companies.

parts.heading: Running the whole test on a fact pattern
parts.voice: direct and exam-focused — addresses the reader as someone about to sit a problem question, moving fast between the doctrines already covered
body: In an exam, privity rarely turns up labelled. It hides inside a fact pattern about a wedding, a building contract, a holiday, or a will — and your job is to work out, methodically, whether the third party has any route to a remedy at all, common law or statutory.

Start by asking whether the 1999 Act applies on the facts as given. If it does, run the s 1 test in full: identification, benefit or express provision, and the s 1(2) intention check. Most exam traps live in s 1(2) — a term that superficially benefits a third party but where the contract's overall structure shows the parties meant only the original promisee to enforce it.

If the 1999 Act is excluded — either expressly, or because the third party cannot satisfy s 1(3) — fall back to the common law routes from earlier in this lesson: is there a distinct legal capacity the claimant could sue in, as in Beswick? Could the promisee's own damages claim be enlarged along Jackson lines? These routes are narrower and less reliable than the statute, but they are not obsolete — the 1999 Act supplements the common law, and does not replace it.

Above all, resist the instinct to treat 'the contract clearly benefits them' as the end of the analysis. Dunlop was decided on facts where the third party's commercial interest in the term was obvious, and it still lost. A benefit, without more, has never been enough — the question is always whether the legal machinery, statutory or common law, actually gives this particular third party a route to court.

components.title: Third-party enforcement — which route, if any?
components.description: A decision path for working out whether a third party can enforce a contract term.

nodes.label: Is the claimant a party to the contract?
Yes → ordinary contract claim, privity is not in issue
No → does the contract expressly exclude the 1999 Act?
Yes, excluded → fall back to common law routes only (agency, trust of promise, Jackson-style damages via the promisee)
No → run s 1: identification under s 1(3), and benefit/express provision under s 1(1), checked against intention under s 1(2)
Conditions satisfied → third party may enforce the term directly under s 1
Conditions not satisfied → fall back to common law routes only

components.textAlternative: First ask if the claimant is already a party to the contract — if so, privity is not in issue. If they are a third party, check whether the contract expressly excludes the 1999 Act. If excluded, only the common law routes (agency, trust of a promise, or enlarged damages recovered by the promisee) remain available. If not excluded, run the full s 1 test: identification under s 1(3), and either express provision or a purported benefit under s 1(1), checked against the parties' intention under s 1(2). If those conditions are satisfied, the third party can enforce the term directly. If not satisfied, fall back to the common law routes only.

interaction.prompt: Aisha's grandmother enters a contract with a building firm to have a garden room built 'for the use and enjoyment of my granddaughter Aisha'. The contract contains no clause excluding the 1999 Act and no express provision letting Aisha sue. The firm builds the room defectively. Analyse whether Aisha can enforce the contract under the 1999 Act.
factsToOrder: Aisha is not a party to the contract
The contract names Aisha and describes the room as for her use and enjoyment
There is no clause excluding the 1999 Act
There is no express term stating Aisha may enforce the contract
The firm built the room defectively

scaffolds.support: Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Aisha, a third party, can enforce the building contract under s 1 of the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999.
modelAnswer.rule: Under s 1(1)(b), a third party may enforce a term that purports to confer a benefit on them, unless s 1(2) shows the parties did not intend it to be enforceable by the third party; under s 1(3) the third party must be identified by name, class, or description.
modelAnswer.application: There is no express provision under s 1(1)(a), so the claim must run under s 1(1)(b). The term plainly purports to confer a benefit on Aisha — the room is built expressly for her use and enjoyment. She is expressly named, satisfying s 1(3). Nothing in the facts suggests the parties intended to exclude third-party enforcement under s 1(2); there is no exclusion clause at all.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Aisha can enforce the term under s 1(1)(b) of the 1999 Act: she is identified, the term purports to benefit her, and nothing rebuts that under s 1(2).

testPool.prompt: State the common law doctrine of privity of contract.
acceptableAnswers: only parties to a contract can sue or be sued on it
a third party has no rights or liabilities under a contract they are not a party to
testPool.modelAnswer: Privity of contract means that only the parties to a contract can sue to enforce it or be sued for breaching it — a third party acquires no rights and incurs no liabilities under it, whatever benefit or burden it carries for them.

testPool.prompt: Which case is the leading common law authority establishing the doctrine of privity in its modern form?
options: Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Co Ltd v Selfridge & Co Ltd
Beswick v Beswick

testPool.prompt: Which of the following was NOT a common law route used to work around privity before the 1999 Act?
options: Suing in a different legal capacity, as in Beswick v Beswick
Recovering enlarged damages reflecting a third party's loss, as in Jackson v Horizon Holidays
Automatically implying a term giving every intended beneficiary a direct right to sue
testPool.trapExplanation: No such automatic implied term existed at common law — that is precisely the gap the 1999 Act was created to fill. The pre-1999 routes were narrow and fact-specific, not a general right.

testPool.prompt: Order the reasoning steps a court follows when a third party seeks to enforce a term under the 1999 Act.
items: Confirm the claimant is not a party to the contract
Check whether the contract expressly excludes the Act
Check express provision or purported benefit under s 1(1), against intention under s 1(2)

testPool.prompt: Section 1(2) of the 1999 Act qualifies the benefit limb in s 1(1)(b). What does it do?
options: It removes enforcement where, on the contract's proper construction, the parties did not intend the term to be enforceable by the third party
It requires the third party to have paid consideration before enforcing the term
It limits third-party enforcement to contracts made in writing

testPool.prompt: In the passage below from Dunlop v Selfridge, highlight the sentence stating the ratio.
testPool.passage: Dunlop had supplied tyres to Dew & Co under a contract requiring resale price undertakings from sub-purchasers. A person who is not a party to a contract cannot take advantage of its provisions, even though the contract was made for his benefit. Dunlop's claim against Selfridge accordingly failed.
testPool.ratioSentence: A person who is not a party to a contract cannot take advantage of its provisions, even though the contract was made for his benefit.

testPool.prompt: A contract between a homeowner and a builder states: 'This clause is for the personal benefit of the homeowner's tenant, Mr Osei, though nothing in this agreement is intended to be enforceable by him.' Can Mr Osei enforce the term under s 1(1)(b)?
options: No — s 1(2) rebuts the benefit presumption because the parties expressly stated they did not intend the term to be enforceable by him
Yes — any term expressed to benefit a named person is automatically enforceable by them
Yes, but only if he can show he relied on the term
testPool.explanation: This is a textbook s 1(2) case: the term purports to benefit Mr Osei, but the parties' express statement of non-enforceability defeats the s 1(1)(b) presumption outright.

testPool.prompt: A shipbuilding contract provides that 'any future purchaser of this vessel' may enforce the warranty clause against the builder. The vessel is later sold to a company that did not exist when the contract was signed. Can that company rely on s 1(3)?
options: No — a third party must exist at the time the contract is made
Yes — s 1(3) expressly allows identification by class or description, and the third party need not exist when the contract is entered into
No — only individuals, not companies, can be third parties under the Act
testPool.explanation: s 1(3) was drafted precisely to cover this situation: identification by description ('any future purchaser') is sufficient, and non-existence at the time of contracting is expressly no bar.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that most closely mirrors the Jackson v Horizon Holidays workaround.
testPool.scenarioText: Priya books a group cookery course for herself and three friends. The course is cancelled halfway through due to the venue's negligence. Priya alone contracted with the cookery school. She sues for breach and claims damages reflecting the disappointment of all four attendees, not just her own.
tappableSpans: Priya books a group cookery course
The course is cancelled halfway through
Priya alone contracted with the cookery school
she sues for breach and claims damages reflecting the disappointment of all four attendees
testPool.correctSpan: she sues for breach and claims damages reflecting the disappointment of all four attendees
testPool.feedbackCorrect: That's the Jackson move exactly — the sole contracting party recovers damages measured by the group's collective loss, without the friends acquiring any claim of their own.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the moment Priya's claim expands beyond her own personal loss to cover everyone's disappointment — that expansion, not the booking or the cancellation itself, is what Jackson stands for.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario more closely mirrors the reasoning that actually succeeded in Beswick v Beswick?
testPool.scenarioA: A widow sues in her personal capacity as the intended beneficiary of an annuity promise her late husband secured for her.
testPool.scenarioB: A widow, appointed administratrix of her late husband's estate, sues to enforce a promise her husband made to the defendant, standing in her husband's own contractual shoes.
testPool.explanation: B captures what actually won in Beswick: the claim succeeded because the widow sued as administratrix, enforcing her husband's own right, not because she was the intended beneficiary — that personal claim, mirrored in A, failed.

testPool.prompt: A father contracts with a driving school for lessons 'for the benefit of my son, Tomas'. The contract expressly states: 'The Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 is excluded; no third party may enforce any term of this agreement.' The driving school provides substandard lessons. Tomas wants to sue. Analyse his position.
factsToOrder: The contract is between the father and the driving school
The term is expressed to benefit Tomas
The contract expressly excludes the 1999 Act
The driving school provides substandard lessons
Tomas is not a party and has no separate legal capacity (such as administratrix) available to him

Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Tomas, a third party expressly excluded from the 1999 Act, has any route to enforce the driving lesson contract.
modelAnswer.rule: The 1999 Act is a default regime that contracting parties may exclude by clear words (s 1(1) read with the Act's general scheme); where excluded, only common law workarounds — such as suing in a different legal capacity, or a contracting party recovering enlarged damages as in Jackson — remain available, and only where the facts support them.
modelAnswer.application: The express exclusion clause removes any s 1 route entirely — Tomas cannot rely on the 1999 Act however clearly the lessons were meant to benefit him. He has no separate legal capacity, such as an estate or agency relationship, that would let him step into his father's contractual shoes as in Beswick. The most realistic route is that his father, as the contracting party, could sue the driving school himself and potentially recover damages reflecting Tomas's own disappointment, along Jackson lines.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Tomas has no direct claim of his own; any remedy depends on his father bringing the claim, potentially recovering damages that reflect Tomas's loss.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that commercial parties are free to exclude the 1999 Act entirely by express words in their contract?
sliderLabels: Not confident — the Act cannot be excluded
Confident — the Act is a default regime that can be excluded
testPool.correctPosition: Confident — the Act is a default regime that can be excluded
testPool.explanation: The 1999 Act supplies a default right of enforcement, not a mandatory one. Commercial contracts very commonly exclude it by express clause, and such exclusion clauses are routinely effective.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best captures the relationship between the 1999 Act and the pre-existing common law on privity?
options: The Act abolished the privity doctrine entirely, replacing it with a general right for anyone affected by a contract to sue on it
The Act created a statutory exception to privity, operating alongside it — privity remains the general rule, and the common law workarounds remain available where the Act does not apply
The Act only applies to consumer contracts, never to commercial ones
testPool.trapExplanation: The tempting error is to treat the 1999 Act as sweeping privity away. It did not: privity remains the default rule, the Act carves out a conditional statutory exception, and the older common law routes (Beswick, Jackson) remain relevant wherever the Act's conditions are not met or the Act is excluded.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is stopping the analysis at 'this term clearly benefits the third party'. A benefit is only the start of the s 1(1)(b) test — check identification under s 1(3), check the parties' intention under s 1(2), and always check first whether the Act has been excluded altogether.
